title: Expected Value
objective: After this level you can work out the average result of a bet over many plays by weighing each outcome by its chance.
summary: A bet's expected value is its average result per play over many plays: multiply each outcome by its chance and add. It is an average, not a promise about any single play.

cards.headline: Heads, you win $3. Tails, you lose $2. Should you play?
cards.body: It feels close. One number settles it: the expected value, the average a bet pays per play if you play it over and over.

cards.headline: Weigh each outcome by its chance, then add
cards.body: Heads and tails each come up half the time, so weigh each result by one half. Winning $3 counts as $1.50. Losing $2 counts as minus $1. Add them: $1.50 minus $1 is 50 cents. That's the expected value of one flip. The recipe works for any bet: multiply each outcome by its probability, then add the results.

cards.headline: An average, not a promise
cards.body: You'll never win exactly 50 cents on a flip. You win $3 or lose $2. Expected value is an average over many plays: play 100 times and you'd expect to finish about $50 ahead, though any real run of flips wanders around that. That's why it's called expected, not guaranteed.

cards.fact: A $2 game with a 1 in 100,000 chance at $100,000 is worth about minus $1 a play.
cards.context: This one comes from a statistics textbook. The prize weighed by its chance is $100,000 ÷ 100,000, or $1 per play. You pay $2. So on average you lose about $1 every time you play. A negative expected value means a game takes back more than it gives. Keep an eye out: the next few levels are full of them.

cards.headline: Expected value: worked out
learned: Weigh each outcome by its chance, then add
The coin game is worth 50 cents a flip
An average over many plays, not a promise
Negative expected value: the game takes more than it gives

questions.prompt: What is a bet's expected value?

options.label: The amount you will win on your next play
options.rationale: Expected value is an average; one play gives an actual outcome.

options.label: Its average result per play over many plays
The biggest prize it can pay
options.rationale: The biggest prize ignores how likely it is.

options.label: The chance that you win
options.rationale: That's the probability, not the value.

questions.explanation: Expected value is the long-run average result per play, found by weighing each outcome by its chance.

questions.prompt: Heads, you win $4. Tails, you lose $2. How does the expected value per flip work out?

options.label: $4 minus $2, which is plus $2
options.rationale: Each outcome must be weighed by its chance, one half.

options.label: Zero, because a coin is fair
options.rationale: A fair coin can still pay unequal amounts.

options.label: $4 × ½ minus $2 × ½, which is plus $1
½ × ½, which is 25 cents
options.rationale: That multiplies the chances and ignores the dollars.

questions.explanation: Weigh each result by one half: $2 minus $1 is plus $1 per flip.

questions.prompt: A game pays $10 if you win, and the odds are 4 to 1 against. On average, the prize is worth _____ per play.

options.rationale: That uses a 1 in 4 chance; 4 to 1 against is 1 in 5.
That weighs the prize by the chance of losing.
That multiplies by the odds instead of the chance.

questions.explanation: Odds of 4 to 1 against are a 1 in 5 chance. $10 × 1/5 = $2 per play.
